subtopic_detail: Brief positional spinning with torsional upbeating nystagmus provoked by a positioning manoeuvre
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 58 year old woman who has had episodes of the room spinning for the past week. Each episode comes on when she rolls onto her right side in bed or tips her head back to hang out washing, builds over a few seconds and settles within half a minute if she stays still.

She feels unsteady and nauseated for a while afterwards but is completely well between episodes. She has no hearing loss, no ringing in the ears and no feeling of fullness in either ear, and no headache. She has had no double vision, slurred speech, weakness or numbness.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76 per minute, blood pressure 128/78 mmHg lying with no postural drop, respiratory rate 15 per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Right Dix Hallpike manoeuvre provokes upbeating torsional nystagmus after a latency of about five seconds that fatigues within thirty seconds and reproduces her vertigo, left Dix Hallpike negative, no spontaneous nystagmus on sitting, cranial nerves intact, gait and limb coordination within normal limits, whispered voice test normal in both ears

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe regular prochlorperazine to be taken for the next two weeks
options.rationale: Vestibular sedatives have a place in the first day or two of severe continuous vertigo such as vestibular neuritis, where vomiting prevents oral intake. In brief positional attacks they treat nothing between episodes, and continued use delays central compensation and causes sedation and drug induced parkinsonism in older people. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Commence betahistine at a standard dose and review her symptoms in a month
options.rationale: Betahistine is used in Meniere disease, which presents with attacks lasting twenty minutes to hours accompanied by fluctuating hearing loss, tinnitus and aural fullness. Her attacks last seconds, are positionally triggered, and her hearing is normal. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Request magnetic resonance imaging of the brain with attention to the posterior fossa
options.rationale: Imaging is needed when nystagmus is purely vertical or direction changing, when it does not fatigue, or when there is any focal neurological sign, since a posterior fossa lesion can mimic positional vertigo. Latency, fatigability and a torsional upbeating pattern in a single head position are all reassuring peripheral features. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Perform a canalith repositioning manoeuvre at this consultation and reassess
options.rationale: Upbeating torsional nystagmus with latency and fatigability on positioning localises displaced otoconia to the posterior semicircular canal on the side tested, and a repositioning manoeuvre returns them to the utricle. A single treatment resolves symptoms in around eight in ten people and can be repeated at the same visit if the manoeuvre is still positive. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Refer for a course of vestibular rehabilitation exercises with a physiotherapist
options.rationale: Vestibular rehabilitation is valuable for persistent imbalance after vestibular neuritis and for people whose positional vertigo recurs despite repositioning. It works by promoting central adaptation over weeks, which is a slower route to the same endpoint when a mechanical problem can be corrected in minutes. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo is the commonest cause of vertigo in general practice and results from otoconia displaced from the utricle into a semicircular canal, most often the posterior canal, where they move under gravity and deflect the cupula. The history is characteristic: attacks lasting seconds to under a minute, triggered by a change in head position relative to gravity such as rolling over, lying down or looking up, with normal hearing and no other neurological symptoms. Diagnosis is made by the Dix Hallpike manoeuvre, and the expected response is upbeating torsional nystagmus with a latency of a few seconds that fatigues on repetition. Treatment is a repositioning manoeuvre, which resolves symptoms in the large majority at the first or second attempt, and medication has no therapeutic role. Features that should prompt imaging are nystagmus that is purely vertical, direction changing or non fatiguing, any focal neurological sign, or vertigo with new headache or neck pain.
key_points: Attacks last under a minute and are triggered by head position relative to gravity
Normal hearing separates it from Meniere disease and labyrinthitis
Latency and fatigability of the nystagmus are peripheral features
A repositioning manoeuvre resolves symptoms in about eighty per cent at one visit
Vestibular sedatives delay compensation and have no therapeutic role here
explanation.pearls: Watch the direction of the nystagmus rather than just whether the patient feels dizzy: upbeating and torsional means the posterior canal and responds to an Epley manoeuvre, whereas horizontal nystagmus that changes direction when the patient rolls from side to side is lateral canal disease and needs a barbecue roll instead.

sources.label: RACGP: Assessment of the dizzy patient
BMJ Best Practice: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo

subtopic_detail: Paroxysmal electric shock facial pain triggered by light touch with an entirely normal neurological examination
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 62 year old man who describes sudden bursts of pain in his right cheek and along his upper jaw that he likens to an electric shock. Each burst lasts a second or two, comes in runs of several minutes, and happens twenty or thirty times a day.

It is set off by shaving, by cold wind on his face and by brushing his teeth, and he has stopped shaving that side and eats only on the left. He has no pain between the attacks, no facial numbness, no ear or eye symptoms and no headache. He saw his dentist last month, who found no dental cause and took radiographs that were normal.

data_table.Examination: Light touch and pinprick sensation equal over all three trigeminal divisions bilaterally, corneal reflex present and symmetrical, masseter and temporalis bulk and power within normal limits, facial movement symmetrical, hearing normal, no cerebellar signs
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, urea creatinine and electrolytes, liver function and inflammatory markers all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Commence amitriptyline at night and increase the dose slowly over four weeks
options.rationale: Tricyclic antidepressants are effective for continuous neuropathic pain such as postherpetic neuralgia and painful diabetic neuropathy, where the mechanism is ongoing ectopic firing. They have not been shown to work for this paroxysmal shock like pain, which responds to sodium channel blockade. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Commence carbamazepine and check the sodium and liver function before starting
options.rationale: Brief electric shock pains in a trigeminal distribution triggered by innocuous stimuli, with a normal examination, are trigeminal neuralgia, and carbamazepine is the only agent with consistent randomised evidence, producing meaningful relief in about seven in ten people. Baseline sodium and liver function are checked because hyponatraemia, hepatitis and marrow suppression are the important adverse effects, and the risk of severe cutaneous reaction is higher in people of Han Chinese, Thai and other South East Asian ancestry who carry a particular tissue type. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Commence gabapentin and titrate the dose upwards over the next three weeks
options.rationale: Gabapentinoids are reasonable second line or add on agents when sodium channel blockers are not tolerated, and they are widely used for other neuropathic pain. Their evidence in trigeminal neuralgia is much weaker than that for carbamazepine, so using them first accepts a lower chance of response. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Commence modified release oxycodone regularly and review the dose in two weeks
options.rationale: Opioids are largely ineffective in this condition because the pain is paroxysmal and over within seconds, so a sustained analgesic level does not match the pain pattern. Long term opioid use in a chronic non cancer condition also brings tolerance, dependence and overdose risk for no demonstrated benefit. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Analgesic)

options.text: Refer to a neurosurgeon for microvascular decompression of the affected nerve
options.rationale: Microvascular decompression gives durable relief in the majority and is the definitive treatment where a vascular loop compresses the nerve root, but it is a posterior fossa craniotomy with risks of hearing loss and facial numbness. It is offered once medical treatment has failed or is not tolerated, not before any drug has been tried. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Trigeminal neuralgia is characterised by recurrent brief paroxysms of severe electric shock like pain confined to one or more trigeminal divisions, most commonly the maxillary and mandibular, precipitated by innocuous stimuli such as chewing, shaving, cold air or teeth brushing. It has a prevalence rising with age, affects women somewhat more often, and is usually caused by a vascular loop compressing the trigeminal root entry zone and demyelinating it. Magnetic resonance imaging is recommended to identify secondary causes, which are suggested by onset before fifty years, bilateral pain, sensory loss on examination, or other cranial nerve involvement, and multiple sclerosis is the most important of these. Carbamazepine is first line and oxcarbazepine is the main alternative with fewer interactions and better tolerability but a higher rate of hyponatraemia. Surgical options, comprising microvascular decompression, stereotactic radiosurgery and percutaneous ablative procedures, are considered when medical treatment fails, and many people present after prolonged and unsuccessful dental treatment.
key_points: Paroxysms last seconds and are triggered by innocuous stimuli in a trigeminal division
A normal sensory examination is expected and its absence suggests a secondary cause
Carbamazepine is the only agent with consistent randomised evidence
Check baseline sodium and liver function, and consider ancestry related skin reaction risk
Onset before fifty, bilateral pain or sensory loss should prompt imaging for demyelination
explanation.pearls: Recheck the sodium two to four weeks after starting carbamazepine and after any dose increase: hyponatraemia from inappropriate antidiuresis develops in up to a quarter of older patients, is often asymptomatic until confusion or a seizure occurs, and is the commonest reason the drug has to be stopped.

subtopic_detail: Proximal muscle aching weeks after starting high intensity statin therapy with a mildly raised creatine kinase
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 64 year old man who had a myocardial infarction and a drug eluting stent placed three months ago and was discharged on atorvastatin, aspirin, ticagrelor, metoprolol and perindopril.

For the past six weeks he has had a dull ache across both thighs and shoulders that is worse after walking the dog and eases with rest. He has no dark urine, no muscle tenderness and no difficulty rising from a chair. He has started no new medication, takes no supplements, and does not drink grapefruit juice. He tells you he has read that statins ruin muscles and wants to stop the tablet permanently.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 62 per minute, blood pressure 124/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: No proximal weakness on formal testing, no muscle tenderness or swelling, no rash, reflexes symmetrical, able to rise from a chair without using his arms
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 320 U/L (less than 200), urea creatinine and electrolytes within normal limits, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, vitamin D within normal limits, low density lipoprotein cholesterol 1.4 mmol/L (target less than 1.8 after an event)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Stop the atorvastatin permanently and commence ezetimibe as a replacement
options.rationale: Ezetimibe is the standard substitute for someone genuinely unable to tolerate any statin, but it lowers low density lipoprotein cholesterol far less and has weaker outcome evidence after an acute coronary syndrome. Abandoning statins after a single unconfirmed reaction gives up the most effective secondary prevention he has. (Source: NHFA and CSANZ: Acute coronary syndromes guideline)
source_refs: NHFA and CSANZ: Acute coronary syndromes guideline

options.text: Continue the atorvastatin unchanged and reassure him that the ache is unrelated
options.rationale: Reassurance alone ignores a symptom that is limiting his exercise and disregards his stated intention to stop, which in practice leads to silent discontinuation. Around half of people who stop a statin because of muscle symptoms tolerate rechallenge, and finding that out requires a structured trial rather than dismissal. (Source: NHFA and CSANZ: Acute coronary syndromes guideline)
source_refs: NHFA and CSANZ: Acute coronary syndromes guideline

options.text: Add coenzyme Q10 supplementation and continue the current statin dose unchanged
options.rationale: Coenzyme Q10 is widely promoted for statin related muscle symptoms on the basis that statins lower its concentration, but randomised trials and meta analyses have not shown it reduces symptoms. Recommending it adds cost and implies a mechanism that the evidence does not support. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Lipid modifying drugs)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook: Lipid modifying drugs

options.text: Request antibodies to hydroxymethylglutaryl coenzyme A reductase before deciding
options.rationale: These antibodies identify immune mediated necrotising myopathy, a rare condition that persists or progresses after the statin is stopped and typically presents with objective proximal weakness and a creatine kinase above ten times the upper limit. A mildly raised level with no weakness does not warrant the test. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Inflammatory myopathy guidance)
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association: Inflammatory myopathy guidance

options.text: Withhold the statin briefly and rechallenge at a lower dose or with another agent
options.rationale: A creatine kinase below four times the upper limit with no objective weakness is muscle symptoms rather than myopathy, and a structured dechallenge and rechallenge distinguishes a true statin effect from unrelated musculoskeletal pain, since symptoms recur on rechallenge in only a minority. Rosuvastatin taken on alternate days or a lower dose of a different agent allows most people to remain on some statin, and combining a reduced dose with ezetimibe preserves the cholesterol target. (Source: NHFA and CSANZ: Acute coronary syndromes guideline)
source_refs: NHFA and CSANZ: Acute coronary syndromes guideline

explanation.summary: Muscle symptoms are reported by up to a fifth of statin users in observational practice, yet blinded randomised crossover studies show that the great majority of these symptoms occur equally on placebo, which is why a structured rechallenge is central to management. The spectrum runs from myalgia with a normal or mildly raised creatine kinase, through myopathy with weakness and a creatine kinase above ten times the upper limit, to rhabdomyolysis with renal impairment and myoglobinuria. Before attributing symptoms to the drug, secondary contributors are checked, including hypothyroidism, vitamin D deficiency, strenuous unaccustomed exercise, alcohol and interacting medications such as macrolides, azoles, verapamil, amiodarone and fibrates. Management of simple muscle symptoms is to withhold the statin until symptoms settle, then rechallenge with the same or a different agent at a lower dose or an intermittent schedule, since most people tolerate some statin. Complete discontinuation is reserved for those with true intolerance to multiple agents, and even then a reduced dose combined with ezetimibe usually achieves the target after an acute coronary syndrome.
key_points: Most reported statin muscle symptoms recur equally on placebo in blinded trials
Creatine kinase below four times the upper limit with no weakness is myalgia, not myopathy
Exclude hypothyroidism, vitamin D deficiency and interacting drugs first
Dechallenge and rechallenge identifies the minority with a genuine statin effect
Most patients tolerate a lower dose or an alternate day schedule of another statin
explanation.pearls: Offer rosuvastatin on alternate days as the rechallenge option: its long half life keeps low density lipoprotein cholesterol suppressed between doses, and intermittent dosing allows around three quarters of people labelled statin intolerant to remain on treatment after a coronary event.

sources.label: NHFA and CSANZ: Acute coronary syndromes guideline
Australian Medicines Handbook: Lipid modifying drugs
Australian Rheumatology Association: Inflammatory myopathy guidance

subtopic_detail: Girdle pain with prolonged morning stiffness and a high inflammatory response without weakness or cranial symptoms
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 71 year old woman with six weeks of pain across both shoulders and both hips that came on over a few days. She says she cannot lift her arms to wash her hair and has to roll out of bed sideways, and that it takes well over an hour each morning before she can move freely.

She has had no jaw ache when chewing, no scalp tenderness when brushing her hair, and no visual disturbance of any kind. She has lost two kilograms and feels generally unwell but has had no fevers, night sweats or cough. She takes no statin and no new medication.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84 per minute, blood pressure 136/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Painful restriction of active shoulder abduction bilaterally with full passive range, no synovitis of the small joints, power 5 out of 5 in all limbs on formal testing, temporal arteries non tender with normal pulsation, no rash
data_table.Investigations: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate 68 mm/h (less than 30), C reactive protein 54 mg/L (less than 5), creatine kinase within normal limits, full blood count shows a normocytic anaemia with haemoglobin 112 g/L (115-155), rheumatoid factor and anti cyclic citrullinated peptide negative, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Commence prednisolone 15 mg daily and review the response within one week
options.rationale: Girdle pain with morning stiffness beyond forty five minutes and a raised inflammatory response in a woman over fifty, with normal power and a normal creatine kinase, is polymyalgia rheumatica, and the treatment is low dose corticosteroid. A dramatic response within a few days at this dose is expected and forms part of the diagnosis, so failure to improve should prompt reconsideration rather than dose escalation. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Polymyalgia rheumatica)

options.text: Commence prednisolone 60 mg daily and arrange urgent temporal artery biopsy
options.rationale: High dose corticosteroid with urgent biopsy is the response to giant cell arteritis, which shares the inflammatory background and overlaps in up to a fifth of cases. It requires cranial features such as new headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness or visual symptoms, and all of those are absent here. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Polymyalgia rheumatica)

options.text: Commence ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily and review again in four weeks
options.rationale: Non steroidal anti inflammatory drugs give only partial relief in this condition and carry gastrointestinal, renal and cardiovascular risk in a woman of this age. A poor response to them is itself a recognised feature that distinguishes the condition from degenerative shoulder disease. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: Commence methotrexate 10 mg weekly with folic acid on the following day
options.rationale: Methotrexate is used as a corticosteroid sparing agent in people who relapse repeatedly, who cannot reduce the dose, or who are at high risk from prolonged steroid exposure. It takes weeks to act and is not used as initial monotherapy. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Polymyalgia rheumatica)

options.text: Commence paracetamol 1 g four times daily and refer her to a physiotherapist
options.rationale: Simple analgesia and exercise are the right approach to bilateral rotator cuff disease or osteoarthritis, which produce shoulder pain without systemic features. They do not treat an inflammatory condition that has produced weight loss, anaemia and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 68 mm/h. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

explanation.summary: Polymyalgia rheumatica occurs almost exclusively in people over fifty, with a peak incidence in the seventies, and presents with relatively abrupt bilateral shoulder and hip girdle pain, morning stiffness lasting more than forty five minutes, and constitutional symptoms with a raised erythrocyte sedimentation rate or C reactive protein. Muscle strength is normal on formal testing despite the patient's sense of weakness, and the creatine kinase is normal, which separates it from inflammatory myositis. Important mimics include late onset rheumatoid arthritis, which involves small joints and is often seropositive, hypothyroidism, statin myopathy, and malignancy, so a poor or partial steroid response should trigger reassessment. Giant cell arteritis coexists in a significant minority and must be asked about at every visit, since visual loss is preventable and irreversible once established. Treatment is prednisolone at 12.5 to 25 mg daily with a slow taper over one to two years, accompanied by bone protection, and relapse during tapering is common.
key_points: Abrupt bilateral girdle pain with morning stiffness over forty five minutes in someone over fifty
Strength is normal on formal testing and the creatine kinase is normal
A dramatic response to low dose prednisolone within days supports the diagnosis
Cranial symptoms must be sought at every visit because they change the dose tenfold
Bone protection is started with the steroid, given one to two years of treatment
explanation.pearls: Tell her to telephone immediately if she develops jaw ache while chewing, scalp tenderness or any visual symptom, and to take prednisolone 60 mg that day: giant cell arteritis emerges during treatment in up to a fifth of patients, and visual loss once established does not recover with any dose.

subtopic_detail: Periprocedural planning before iodinated contrast in a diabetic patient with moderately reduced kidney function
stem:
You are the medical registrar asked to advise before a 68 year old man with type 2 diabetes attends for a computed tomography coronary angiogram with iodinated contrast next week.

He takes metformin, perindopril and rosuvastatin, and has stable exertional chest tightness under investigation. He is eating and drinking normally, has had no vomiting or diarrhoea, and is on no diuretic or non steroidal anti inflammatory drug. He has had contrast for a computed tomography scan two years ago without any problem.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 70 per minute, blood pressure 134/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Euvolaemic with moist mucous membranes, jugular venous pressure not elevated, no peripheral oedema, chest clear
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 148 micromol/L (60-110) with estimated glomerular filtration rate 38 mL/min/1.73m2 stable across three measurements over a year, potassium 4.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), bicarbonate 24 mmol/L (22-28), haemoglobin A1c 52 mmol/mol, urine albumin creatinine ratio 18 mg/mmol

lead_in: What is the most appropriate periprocedural plan?

options.text: Withhold the metformin for 48 hours before and 48 hours after the contrast study
options.rationale: Withholding metformin around contrast is advised when the estimated glomerular filtration rate is below 30 mL/min/1.73m2, or with intra arterial contrast to the renal arteries, where a contrast related fall in function could allow metformin to accumulate. At 38 mL/min/1.73m2 with stable function it is not required, and four days without treatment worsens glycaemic control for no benefit. (Source: RANZCR and RACGP: Iodinated contrast media guideline)
source_refs: RANZCR and RACGP: Iodinated contrast media guideline

options.text: Give oral N acetylcysteine on the day before and the day of the contrast study
options.rationale: N acetylcysteine was widely used on the basis of small early trials, but large randomised evidence including a trial of more than five thousand patients found no reduction in contrast associated kidney injury, dialysis or death. It is no longer recommended in current guidance. (Source: RANZCR and RACGP: Iodinated contrast media guideline)
source_refs: RANZCR and RACGP: Iodinated contrast media guideline

options.text: Give intravenous isotonic saline around the study and continue the metformin
options.rationale: Volume expansion with isotonic saline before and after contrast is the only intervention with consistent evidence for reducing contrast associated kidney injury, and it is indicated at an estimated glomerular filtration rate below 45 mL/min/1.73m2. Metformin is continued because the threshold for withholding it with intravenous contrast is an estimated glomerular filtration rate below 30 mL/min/1.73m2. (Source: RANZCR and RACGP: Iodinated contrast media guideline)
source_refs: RANZCR and RACGP: Iodinated contrast media guideline

options.text: Give an infusion of isotonic sodium bicarbonate instead of saline before the study
options.rationale: Bicarbonate was proposed to reduce free radical injury in the medulla by alkalinising tubular fluid, and early trials suggested benefit. Head to head randomised comparison has shown no advantage over isotonic saline, which is cheaper, more available and carries no risk of alkalosis. (Source: RANZCR and RACGP: Iodinated contrast media guideline)
source_refs: RANZCR and RACGP: Iodinated contrast media guideline

options.text: Cancel the contrast study and request a stress echocardiogram in its place
options.rationale: Choosing a test that avoids contrast is appropriate when kidney function is severely impaired and the alternative answers the clinical question equally well. Cancelling here would deny him the anatomical information that computed tomography coronary angiography provides, for a risk that is manageable with hydration. (Source: NHFA and CSANZ: Chest pain guideline)
source_refs: NHFA and CSANZ: Chest pain guideline

explanation.summary: Contrast associated acute kidney injury is far less common than historically believed, and much of the apparent risk in older observational studies reflected the underlying illness of patients receiving contrast rather than the contrast itself. Risk rises with pre existing chronic kidney disease, particularly below 30 mL/min/1.73m2, and with diabetic kidney disease, hypovolaemia, heart failure, high contrast volume and intra arterial administration. Intravenous volume expansion with isotonic saline is the only preventive measure supported by consistent evidence, and both N acetylcysteine and sodium bicarbonate have failed to show benefit in adequately powered trials. Metformin is not nephrotoxic, and the concern is accumulation with lactic acidosis if kidney function falls, so it is withheld around contrast only below an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 30 mL/min/1.73m2 or with intra arterial studies involving the renal circulation. Angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors and receptor blockers are generally continued, while diuretics and non steroidal anti inflammatory drugs are withheld where practical, and kidney function is rechecked at around 48 to 72 hours in higher risk patients.
key_points: Isotonic saline volume expansion is the only preventive measure with consistent evidence
N acetylcysteine and sodium bicarbonate have failed in adequately powered trials
Metformin is withheld with intravenous contrast only below 30 mL/min/1.73m2
Intra arterial contrast carries a higher risk than intravenous contrast
Recheck kidney function at 48 to 72 hours in higher risk patients
explanation.pearls: Withhold the diuretic and any non steroidal anti inflammatory drug rather than the metformin: volume depletion is the modifiable risk factor that actually drives contrast associated kidney injury, whereas stopping metformin at an estimated glomerular filtration rate above 30 mL/min/1.73m2 protects nobody and leaves diabetes untreated for four days.

sources.label: RANZCR and RACGP: Iodinated contrast media guideline
NHFA and CSANZ: Chest pain guideline

subtopic_detail: Request to discontinue a six monthly antiresorptive injection after several years of improving bone density
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 73 year old woman who has had six monthly denosumab injections for four years after a wrist fracture. Her most recent bone density scan shows the T score at the lumbar spine has improved from minus 3.1 to minus 2.2.

She has had no further fractures, takes calcium in her diet and a daily vitamin D supplement, and walks daily. She tells you she feels the problem is now fixed, dislikes injections, and has decided not to have the next one, which is due in three weeks. She takes no corticosteroid and has had no dental problems.

data_table.Examination: Height unchanged from two years ago, no thoracic kyphosis, no spinal tenderness, gait steady with no falls in the past year
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.38 mmol/L (2.20-2.65), 25 hydroxyvitamin D 78 nmol/L (greater than 50), creatinine and estimated glomerular filtration rate within normal limits, bone density T score minus 2.2 at the lumbar spine and minus 2.4 at the femoral neck

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice?

options.text: Agree to stop the injections now and repeat her bone density scan in two years
options.rationale: A drug holiday after several years is reasonable practice with bisphosphonates, which bind to bone and continue to act for years after the last dose. Denosumab has no skeletal retention, so its effect stops completely within months and simply ceasing it leaves the skeleton unprotected. (Source: Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management guideline)
source_refs: Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management guideline

options.text: Explain that stopping requires transition to a bisphosphonate to prevent bone loss
options.rationale: Stopping denosumab produces a rebound rise in bone resorption that returns bone density to baseline within about twelve months and carries a risk of multiple vertebral fractures, which occur in roughly one in twenty women who discontinue. Giving a bisphosphonate at the time the next injection would have been due substantially reduces that rebound, so the discussion is about how to stop safely rather than whether she may. (Source: Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management guideline)
source_refs: Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management guideline

options.text: Extend the interval between injections to twelve months as a compromise measure
options.rationale: Spacing the doses out sounds like a middle path but the antiresorptive effect wanes at around seven months, so an extended interval produces recurring windows of rebound resorption. Delays beyond a month are associated with increased vertebral fracture risk. (Source: Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management guideline)
source_refs: Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management guideline

options.text: Stop the injections and continue calcium and vitamin D as her only treatment
options.rationale: Calcium and vitamin D are supportive measures that ensure substrate for mineralisation and correct deficiency, but they do not prevent the rebound and have minimal antifracture effect on their own. Relying on them here would leave a woman with a previous fracture unprotected during the highest risk period. (Source: Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management guideline)
source_refs: Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management guideline

options.text: Continue the injections indefinitely without any planned review of treatment
options.rationale: Continuing denosumab long term is appropriate for many patients since benefit is maintained for at least ten years, but treatment still needs periodic review of fracture risk, dental health and kidney function. Framing it as indefinite and unreviewable also disregards her clearly stated wish to stop injections. (Source: Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management guideline)
source_refs: Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management guideline

explanation.summary: Denosumab is a monoclonal antibody against receptor activator of nuclear factor kappa B ligand that potently suppresses osteoclast formation and survival, and unlike bisphosphonates it is not incorporated into bone matrix. Its effect therefore reverses completely once dosing stops, producing a rebound increase in bone turnover that exceeds pretreatment levels and returns bone density to baseline within about a year. The clinically important consequence is a risk of multiple spontaneous vertebral fractures, reported in around five per cent of women who discontinue, typically within nine to eighteen months and often affecting several vertebrae at once. Discontinuation is therefore always planned, with a bisphosphonate given at the time the next injection would have been due, and doses should not be delayed beyond about a month. Hypocalcaemia is the other important consideration, particularly in chronic kidney disease or vitamin D deficiency, so calcium and vitamin D status are confirmed before each dose, and dental assessment precedes treatment because of the risk of osteonecrosis of the jaw.
key_points: Denosumab is not retained in bone and its effect fully reverses on stopping
Rebound resorption returns bone density to baseline within about twelve months
Multiple vertebral fractures occur in around five per cent of those who discontinue
A bisphosphonate is given when the next injection would have been due
Doses should not be delayed beyond about a month
explanation.pearls: Treat a missed denosumab appointment with the same urgency as a missed anticoagulant dose in a patient with a mechanical valve: the fracture risk climbs from around seven months after the last injection, and most rebound vertebral fractures occur in people who simply stopped attending rather than in those who stopped on advice.

sources.label: Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management guideline

subtopic_detail: Prolonged fever with hepatitis and negative blood cultures in an abattoir worker with no travel history
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 38 year old man from a regional New South Wales town with twelve days of daily fevers to 39 degrees Celsius, drenching night sweats, severe frontal headache and aching in his thighs and back.

He works on the slaughter floor of an abattoir processing sheep and cattle and has done so for six years. He has not travelled outside Australia, has no recent tick bite and has seen no rash. He has had no cough, no breathlessness, no diarrhoea and no dysuria. His general practitioner gave him amoxicillin a week ago with no effect.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96 per minute, blood pressure 122/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 38.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Unwell and sweaty, no rash and no eschar, no lymphadenopathy, liver edge palpable 2 cm below the costal margin and mildly tender, no splenomegaly, no murmur, chest clear
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 6.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), platelets 128 x10^9/L (150-400), alanine aminotransferase 186 U/L (less than 40), alkaline phosphatase 148 U/L (30-110), bilirubin within normal limits, C reactive protein 96 mg/L (less than 5), two sets of blood cultures sterile at 72 hours, malaria thick and thin films negative, chest radiograph normal, transthoracic echocardiogram shows no vegetation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence intravenous ceftriaxone and repeat the blood cultures before dosing
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone is the standard empirical choice for a septic patient with a suspected bacterial focus and would cover most organisms that grow in bottles. The organism responsible here is an obligate intracellular bacterium that does not grow in routine blood culture, and beta lactams have no activity against it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Commence oral azithromycin to cover atypical community acquired pneumonia
options.rationale: Macrolides cover the atypical respiratory pathogens and are part of moderate severity pneumonia regimens, and they have modest activity against this organism. He has no cough, breathlessness or radiographic infiltrate, and a macrolide is inferior to the tetracycline that is specifically recommended. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Arrange percutaneous liver biopsy to establish the cause of the hepatitis
options.rationale: Liver biopsy can show the doughnut granuloma characteristic of this infection and is occasionally used in prolonged fever of unknown origin. It is invasive, and paired serology establishes the diagnosis non invasively in a patient whose occupational exposure and clinical picture already point strongly to it. (Source: CDNA: Q fever national guidelines)

options.text: Withhold antimicrobial treatment until the serological results become available
options.rationale: Waiting for a result before treating is defensible when the patient is stable and the diagnosis would change management dangerously. Serology is often negative in the first one to two weeks of illness and requires a convalescent sample two to three weeks later, so waiting means several more weeks of fever and a higher risk of chronic infection. (Source: CDNA: Q fever national guidelines)

options.text: Commence oral doxycycline and request acute and convalescent phase serology
options.rationale: An abattoir worker with prolonged fever, severe headache, hepatitis and sterile blood cultures has Q fever until proven otherwise, since the organism is an obligate intracellular bacterium that will not grow in routine culture and is acquired by inhaling aerosols from birth products of infected sheep, cattle and goats. Doxycycline is the treatment of choice and is started empirically because acute serology is frequently negative early and the diagnosis is confirmed by a rise in titre on the convalescent sample. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Q fever is caused by Coxiella burnetii, an obligate intracellular bacterium that is highly infectious and survives in the environment as a spore like form, and Australia has among the highest reported incidences in the world. Transmission is by inhalation of aerosols from birth fluids, placental tissue, urine and faeces of infected livestock, so abattoir workers, farmers, shearers, veterinarians, stock transporters and their household contacts are the risk groups, and no animal contact is reported in a substantial minority because the organism travels on dust and wind. Acute illness is an undifferentiated febrile illness with prominent severe headache, myalgia and sweats, often with hepatitis or an atypical pneumonia, and routine blood cultures are sterile because the organism does not grow in them. Diagnosis is serological, with polymerase chain reaction useful in the first two weeks, and treatment is doxycycline for two weeks. Chronic Q fever, which presents as culture negative endocarditis or vascular infection months to years later, is the reason follow up matters, and it is more likely in those with valvular disease, vascular grafts, immunosuppression or pregnancy. An effective vaccine is available in Australia and must be preceded by skin testing and serology, since giving it to someone with prior exposure causes severe local reactions.
key_points: Abattoir, farm, shearing and veterinary work are the classic Australian exposures
Severe headache with hepatitis and sterile blood cultures is the typical picture
The organism does not grow in routine blood culture bottles
Doxycycline is started empirically because early serology is often negative
Chronic infection presents as culture negative endocarditis months to years later
explanation.pearls: Arrange pre vaccination skin testing and serology before offering the Q fever vaccine to his workmates: vaccinating someone with prior exposure causes a severe local reaction that can ulcerate and leave a permanent scar, which is why the vaccine is never given without that two step screening.

subtopic_detail: Progressive thoracic back pain with a sensory level and upper motor neurone signs in metastatic prostate cancer
stem:
You are the medical registrar seeing a 68 year old man with prostate cancer on androgen deprivation therapy who has had three weeks of mid back pain. The pain is worse at night, wakes him, and is aggravated by coughing and by lying flat.

Over the past four days his legs have felt heavy and he has begun holding the rail to climb the stairs at home. He is passing urine normally with no hesitancy or incontinence and has had no constipation. His last prostate specific antigen three months ago was rising.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82 per minute, blood pressure 132/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Tenderness on percussion over the mid thoracic spine, power 4 out of 5 in hip flexion and knee extension bilaterally, knee and ankle reflexes brisk with bilateral extensor plantar responses, sensory level to pinprick at the level of the umbilicus, normal anal tone, bladder not palpable
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.44 mmol/L (2.20-2.65), full blood count and renal function within normal limits, alkaline phosphatase 310 U/L (30-110), post void bladder scan shows 40 mL residual

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give high dose dexamethasone now and arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the whole spine
options.rationale: Night pain aggravated by coughing and lying flat with brisk reflexes, extensor plantars and a sensory level is cord compression, and corticosteroid is given immediately on clinical suspicion because it reduces vasogenic oedema while imaging is arranged. The whole spine is imaged rather than the symptomatic level because around a third of patients have compression at more than one level, and treating only the level that hurts leaves a second lesion behind. (Source: eviQ: Malignant spinal cord compression)

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the lumbar spine within the next 24 hours
options.rationale: A lumbar study is what cauda equina syndrome requires, which is signalled by saddle anaesthesia, reduced anal tone, urinary retention and flaccid areflexic weakness. His brisk reflexes, extensor plantars and a sensory level at the umbilicus localise the lesion to the thoracic cord, well above the region a lumbar sequence would cover. (Source: eviQ: Malignant spinal cord compression)

options.text: Request plain radiographs of the thoracic spine and a whole body bone scan
options.rationale: Bone scintigraphy maps the skeletal burden of disease and plain films may show vertebral collapse or pedicle erosion, so both have a role in staging. Neither demonstrates the soft tissue and cord itself, and normal films in this situation are falsely reassuring in a substantial minority. (Source: eviQ: Malignant spinal cord compression)

options.text: Refer for urgent radiotherapy to the painful vertebral level before any imaging
options.rationale: Radiotherapy is the usual definitive treatment for cord compression from a radiosensitive tumour and is delivered urgently, but it requires imaging to define the levels to be treated and to identify whether surgical decompression and stabilisation is preferable. Treating the level that hurts without imaging risks missing a second compressive lesion. (Source: eviQ: Malignant spinal cord compression)

options.text: Prescribe opioid analgesia and arrange outpatient imaging within the coming week
options.rationale: Analgesia is certainly required but outpatient scheduling misjudges the timeframe, since neurological function deteriorates over hours to days and recovery depends almost entirely on the deficit at the time treatment begins. A man who is already weak has days rather than a week. (Source: eviQ: Malignant spinal cord compression)

explanation.summary: Malignant spinal cord compression complicates around five per cent of cancers, most often from prostate, breast, lung and myeloma, and arises when vertebral metastases extend into the epidural space or a pathological collapse retropulses bone. Pain precedes neurological signs by weeks in the majority, and the pattern that should prompt urgent assessment is progressive back pain that is worse at night, worse on coughing or straining, or worse when lying flat. Once motor signs appear, function can be lost within hours, and the single strongest predictor of walking afterwards is whether the patient is walking when treatment starts, which is why corticosteroid is given on suspicion rather than after confirmation. Magnetic resonance imaging of the whole spine is the investigation of choice because multiple levels are involved in roughly a third of cases. Definitive treatment is radiotherapy for radiosensitive tumours or surgical decompression with stabilisation where the spine is unstable, where there is bone retropulsion, or where the tumour is radioresistant, and bisphosphonate or denosumab therapy is considered for ongoing skeletal protection.
key_points: Back pain worse at night, on coughing or lying flat is the warning sign before deficit
Brisk reflexes with extensor plantars and a sensory level localise to the cord
Corticosteroid is given on clinical suspicion, before imaging confirms it
The whole spine is imaged since about a third have compression at multiple levels
Ambulatory status at the start of treatment predicts walking afterwards
explanation.pearls: Escalate on the pain rather than waiting for the weakness: pain precedes neurological signs by a median of around seven weeks, and once a patient with cord compression has lost the ability to walk, fewer than one in ten will walk again regardless of how quickly radiotherapy is then delivered.

sources.label: Cancer Council Australia: Prostate cancer management
BMJ Best Practice: Malignant spinal cord compression

subtopic_detail: Severe cavitating pneumonia in a poorly controlled diabetic during the tropical wet season after soil exposure
stem:
You are the medical registrar in a Darwin hospital admitting a 52 year old man in February with five days of fever, productive cough and pleuritic chest pain that have worsened rapidly over the past day.

He has type 2 diabetes managed with metformin and gliclazide and last had his glycated haemoglobin measured a year ago. He operates earthmoving machinery and has been clearing flooded ground for the past fortnight, and he has several healing abrasions on both shins from working in the mud. He has had no overseas travel and is not immunosuppressed.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 126 per minute, blood pressure 88/52 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 per minute, SpO2 89 per cent on 6 L per minute via face mask, temperature 39.2 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Confused and peripherally shut down, bronchial breathing at the right upper zone, several healing abrasions on both shins with no surrounding cellulitis, no murmur, no rash
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 19.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), creatinine 168 micromol/L (60-110), lactate 3.6 mmol/L (less than 2.0), glucose 18.2 mmol/L, glycated haemoglobin 84 mmol/mol, chest radiograph shows dense right upper lobe consolidation with an early cavity, blood cultures taken and pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin with intravenous doxycycline
options.rationale: Benzylpenicillin with doxycycline covers pneumococcus and the atypical pathogens and suits mild community acquired pneumonia in a low risk patient. It does not treat the tropical environmental organism that this presentation points to, and it is inadequate cover for septic shock. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone with intravenous azithromycin
options.rationale: This is the standard Australian regimen for severe community acquired pneumonia outside the tropics and would be right in Melbourne or Sydney. The organism that causes this syndrome in the wet season north is intrinsically resistant to ceftriaxone, which is precisely why the tropical regimen differs. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous flucloxacillin with intravenous vancomycin
options.rationale: Antistaphylococcal cover is reasonable to consider given cavitation and skin breaks, since staphylococcal pneumonia cavitates and can follow bacteraemia from a skin source. It leaves the environmental Gram negative organism untreated, and mortality in that infection rises sharply with each hour of ineffective therapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous meropenem with trimethoprim sulfamethoxazole
options.rationale: Severe cavitating pneumonia with septic shock in a poorly controlled diabetic exposed to wet season soil and surface water in the tropical north is melioidosis, and a carbapenem is the preferred intensive phase agent when there is septic shock or intensive care admission, with ceftazidime the alternative in less severe disease. Trimethoprim with sulfamethoxazole is added for deep seated or severe infection and then continues as eradication therapy for three to six months, without which relapse is common. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous ticarcillin with clavulanate and gentamicin
options.rationale: A beta lactam with a beta lactamase inhibitor combined with an aminoglycoside is a plausible broad regimen for severe Gram negative sepsis and was historically used in tropical practice. Burkholderia pseudomallei is intrinsically resistant to gentamicin and to aminoglycosides generally, so half of this combination contributes nothing and the other half is not an agent with established efficacy against it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Melioidosis is caused by Burkholderia pseudomallei, an environmental Gram negative bacterium found in soil and surface water across northern Australia, and the great majority of cases present during the wet season between November and April. Infection follows percutaneous inoculation through skin breaks, inhalation of aerosolised organisms during heavy rain and wind, or ingestion, and around eighty per cent of patients have a recognised risk factor, with diabetes the commonest, followed by hazardous alcohol use, chronic kidney disease, chronic lung disease and immunosuppression. Pneumonia is the most frequent presentation, often with upper lobe consolidation and cavitation, and up to half of patients are bacteraemic with a substantial proportion presenting in septic shock. The organism is intrinsically resistant to penicillins, ceftriaxone, gentamicin and most other aminoglycosides, so the standard severe community acquired pneumonia regimen fails, and this is the single most important reason to identify the syndrome at presentation. Treatment has two phases: an intensive intravenous phase of at least two weeks with meropenem or ceftazidime, extended for deep seated infection, followed by eradication therapy with trimethoprim and sulfamethoxazole for three to six months, since relapse rates without it are high.
key_points: Wet season soil and surface water exposure in northern Australia is the key history
Diabetes is the commonest predisposing condition and is present in around half
Upper lobe consolidation with cavitation and septic shock is the classic presentation
The organism is intrinsically resistant to ceftriaxone, penicillins and aminoglycosides
Eradication therapy for three to six months follows the intravenous intensive phase
explanation.pearls: Tell the laboratory that melioidosis is suspected when you send the cultures: Burkholderia pseudomallei is readily dismissed as a contaminant or misidentified by automated systems, it is a recognised cause of laboratory acquired infection requiring specific containment, and alerting the laboratory changes both the identification pathway and staff safety.

subtopic_detail: Core temperature in the twenties with bradycardia and a J wave on the electrocardiogram after a night outdoors
stem:
You are the emergency registrar receiving a 74 year old man found at dawn on a park bench after an overnight minimum of 2 degrees Celsius. He had left his nursing home the previous afternoon and had been missing for about sixteen hours.

He is drowsy and confused but opens his eyes to voice and moves all four limbs. He is no longer shivering. His clothing is damp and has been removed and he has been covered with blankets.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 38 per minute, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 8 per minute, SpO2 unable to be recorded reliably due to poor peripheral perfusion, oesophageal temperature 28.5 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Drowsy with a Glasgow Coma Scale of 12, cold and pale peripheries with no shivering, muscle tone increased, pupils sluggish and equal, no head injury, no focal neurology, no signs of frostbite
data_table.Investigations: Electrocardiogram shows sinus bradycardia at 38 per minute with a positive deflection at the junction of the QRS complex and the ST segment in the lateral leads, potassium 4.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), glucose 6.4 mmol/L (3.5-7.8), venous pH 7.28, thyroid function pending, alcohol not detected

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Give atropine intravenously to correct the bradycardia and repeat if needed
options.rationale: Atropine treats bradycardia mediated by vagal tone, which is not the mechanism here, since the hypothermic sinus node is intrinsically slowed and unresponsive to antimuscarinic blockade. A slow rate at this temperature is a physiologically appropriate match to reduced metabolic demand and should be left alone. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline: Hypothermia)

options.text: Apply transcutaneous pacing to raise the heart rate towards a normal range
options.rationale: Pacing is used for haemodynamically significant bradycardia from conduction disease, and it is avoided in hypothermia because the myocardium is highly irritable and electrical stimulation can precipitate ventricular fibrillation. Perfusion is adequate at this rate for a metabolic rate reduced by cold. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline: Hypothermia)

options.text: Begin active external rewarming with warmed intravenous fluid and minimal handling
options.rationale: At a core temperature of 28.5 degrees Celsius with a perfusing rhythm, forced air warming over the trunk combined with warmed intravenous crystalloid rewarms at a safe rate while the patient is moved as little as possible, because mechanical stimulation of an irritable myocardium can precipitate ventricular fibrillation. Warmed fluid is also needed because vasodilatation during rewarming unmasks the volume depletion produced by cold induced diuresis. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline: Hypothermia)

options.text: Insert a central venous catheter via the subclavian route for warmed fluid delivery
options.rationale: Central access allows rapid delivery of warmed fluid and is used in severe cases, but a guidewire advanced into the right atrium is a recognised trigger for ventricular fibrillation in a cold irritable heart. Femoral access is preferred when a central line is genuinely required at this temperature. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline: Hypothermia)

options.text: Immerse him in a hot water bath to raise the core temperature as quickly as possible
options.rationale: Rapid surface rewarming of the limbs opens peripheral vascular beds and returns cold acidotic blood to the core, which can cause a further fall in core temperature and circulatory collapse. Rewarming is therefore directed at the trunk, and monitoring during the process is impossible in a bath. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline: Hypothermia)

explanation.summary: Accidental hypothermia is graded by core temperature, with mild disease from 32 to 35 degrees Celsius where shivering is preserved, moderate from 28 to 32 degrees where shivering ceases and conscious state declines, and severe below 28 degrees where the patient may appear dead. The electrocardiographic hallmark is the Osborn or J wave, a positive deflection at the junction of the QRS complex and the ST segment, and its height broadly tracks the severity of the hypothermia. The cold myocardium is profoundly irritable, so rough handling, unnecessary movement, central line guidewires and pacing can all precipitate ventricular fibrillation, which is refractory to defibrillation and to drugs until the core temperature rises. Rewarming is graded to severity, with passive external methods for mild cases, active external truncal warming plus warmed intravenous fluid for moderate cases, and extracorporeal rewarming for severe hypothermia with cardiac instability or arrest. In cardiac arrest the rule is that resuscitation continues until the core temperature reaches at least 32 to 34 degrees Celsius, since full neurological recovery has been documented after prolonged hypothermic arrest and death is not confirmed until the patient is warm.
key_points: The J wave at the QRS and ST junction is the electrocardiographic hallmark
The cold myocardium is irritable, so handling, pacing and guidewires risk fibrillation
Rewarm the trunk rather than the limbs to avoid an afterdrop in core temperature
Warmed fluid is needed because rewarming vasodilatation unmasks volume depletion
Resuscitation continues until the core temperature reaches 32 to 34 degrees Celsius
explanation.pearls: Ask why he was outdoors rather than treating the temperature alone: in an older Australian patient hypothermia is usually secondary to a fall, sepsis, hypoglycaemia, hypothyroidism or a sedative, and the precipitant determines whether he survives the next week once he has been rewarmed.

subtopic_detail: Symptomatic hypocalcaemia after parathyroidectomy with a low phosphate and a high alkaline phosphatase
stem:
You are the medical registrar called to the surgical ward two days after a 62 year old woman underwent parathyroidectomy for primary hyperparathyroidism. She complains of tingling around her mouth and in her fingertips and says her hands keep cramping.

Before surgery she had bone pain, a corrected calcium of 3.12 mmol/L and a markedly elevated parathyroid hormone, and imaging had shown a single enlarged gland. She takes no other medication and has had no wound problems, no fever and no voice change.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88 per minute, blood pressure 122/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Trousseau sign positive after one minute of cuff inflation, Chvostek sign present, no stridor, no wound haematoma, no carpopedal spasm at rest
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 1.68 mmol/L (2.20-2.65), phosphate 0.54 mmol/L (0.80-1.50), magnesium 0.58 mmol/L (0.70-1.10), alkaline phosphatase 620 U/L (30-110), parathyroid hormone 2.4 pmol/L (1.6-6.9), 25 hydroxyvitamin D 46 nmol/L, electrocardiogram shows a corrected QT interval of 490 ms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence oral calcium carbonate alone and recheck the calcium in the morning
options.rationale: Oral calcium is the mainstay of longer term replacement and will be needed in large doses for weeks. It acts too slowly for symptomatic hypocalcaemia with a prolonged corrected QT interval, and it will not correct the concurrent magnesium deficiency that is impairing the response. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Return her to theatre for exploration of the remaining parathyroid glands
options.rationale: Reoperation is considered for persistent or recurrent hyperparathyroidism, meaning a calcium that fails to fall after surgery. Her calcium has fallen steeply, which indicates the operation achieved its purpose rather than that something was missed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Commence teriparatide by daily subcutaneous injection to replace the missing hormone
options.rationale: Parathyroid hormone analogues are used in chronic hypoparathyroidism that cannot be controlled with calcium and active vitamin D, and they would be logical if the gland remnants had failed. Her parathyroid hormone is within the reference range, showing the remaining glands are working and the calcium is being consumed elsewhere. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Treat as surgical hypoparathyroidism with calcium and calcitriol and monitor daily
options.rationale: Surgical hypoparathyroidism is the other cause of postoperative hypocalcaemia and is treated with exactly these drugs, so the treatments overlap substantially. It is distinguished by a low or undetectable parathyroid hormone and a high phosphate, because absent hormone means phosphate is retained, whereas her phosphate is low and her hormone is measurable. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Give intravenous calcium gluconate with calcitriol and replace the magnesium
options.rationale: A low calcium with a low phosphate, a very high alkaline phosphatase and a measurable parathyroid hormone is hungry bone syndrome, in which bone stripped of longstanding excess hormone drive takes up calcium, phosphate and magnesium avidly. Symptomatic hypocalcaemia with a prolonged corrected QT interval requires intravenous calcium, calcitriol is given because it accelerates gut absorption without waiting on renal hydroxylation, and magnesium is replaced because hypomagnesaemia both impairs parathyroid hormone release and blocks its action at the receptor. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Hypocalcaemia after parathyroidectomy has two distinct causes that are separated by the phosphate and the parathyroid hormone level. Surgical hypoparathyroidism reflects removal of or damage to the remaining glands and shows a low or undetectable hormone with a high phosphate, since parathyroid hormone normally promotes renal phosphate excretion. Hungry bone syndrome reflects rapid remineralisation of a skeleton that has been demineralised by years of excess hormone, and it shows a low phosphate and a low magnesium alongside the low calcium because all three are being taken into bone, with a measurable hormone level. The strongest predictors of hungry bone are a high preoperative alkaline phosphatase, marked preoperative hypercalcaemia, a large adenoma, radiological bone disease and older age. Treatment is intravenous calcium for symptoms or a prolonged corrected QT interval, then large oral doses of calcium with an active vitamin D analogue, together with magnesium replacement, and requirements can remain high for weeks to months until the skeleton is repleted. Correcting magnesium is essential because hypomagnesaemia causes refractory hypocalcaemia that does not respond to calcium alone.
key_points: Phosphate separates the two causes: low in hungry bone, high in hypoparathyroidism
A measurable parathyroid hormone shows the remaining glands are functioning
A high preoperative alkaline phosphatase is the strongest predictor of hungry bone
Intravenous calcium is for symptoms, tetany or a prolonged corrected QT interval
Hypomagnesaemia causes refractory hypocalcaemia and must be corrected in parallel
explanation.pearls: Check the magnesium before concluding that calcium replacement has failed: magnesium below about 0.6 mmol/L both blocks parathyroid hormone secretion and makes the receptor unresponsive to it, so calcium given without magnesium replacement produces a resistant hypocalcaemia that no amount of further calcium will correct.

subtopic_detail: Visual blurring and mucosal bleeding with dilated segmented retinal veins and a very high immunoglobulin M paraprotein
stem:
You are the haematology registrar seeing a 71 year old man referred with six weeks of headache, blurred vision and ringing in his ears, along with nosebleeds and gums that bleed when he cleans his teeth. He has lost four kilograms and is breathless climbing a flight of stairs.

The referring doctor has arranged two units of red cells to be transfused this afternoon for the anaemia and has asked you to review him afterwards. He has no chest pain, no melaena and no haematuria, and takes no anticoagulant or antiplatelet drug.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92 per minute, blood pressure 138/84 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 per minute, SpO2 96 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Pale, with non tender lymphadenopathy in both axillae and a spleen palpable 3 cm below the costal margin, fundoscopy shows dilated tortuous retinal veins with segmental constrictions and scattered flame haemorrhages, no focal neurology, chest clear with no added heart sounds
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 72 g/L (130-180), white cell count 6.1 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), platelets 118 x10^9/L (150-400), blood film shows marked rouleaux, erythrocyte sedimentation rate greater than 140 mm/h, total protein 112 g/L (60-80) with albumin 32 g/L (35-50), serum immunoglobulin M paraprotein 58 g/L, creatinine and corrected calcium within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Arrange urgent plasma exchange and defer the planned red cell transfusion
options.rationale: Headache, visual blurring, tinnitus and mucosal bleeding with dilated segmented retinal veins and an immunoglobulin M paraprotein of 58 g/L is symptomatic hyperviscosity, and plasma exchange removes the responsible protein within hours because immunoglobulin M is largely confined to the intravascular space. Transfusion is deliberately deferred because adding red cell mass raises whole blood viscosity further and can precipitate stroke or visual loss in a patient whose anaemia is chronic and being tolerated. (Source: HSANZ: Waldenstrom macroglobulinaemia guidance)

options.text: Proceed with the two units of red cells and reassess the symptoms afterwards
options.rationale: A haemoglobin of 72 g/L would ordinarily prompt transfusion, and the anaemia is genuine and contributing to his breathlessness. Raising the haematocrit in the presence of a very high paraprotein increases viscosity disproportionately, and transfusion before viscosity is reduced is a recognised precipitant of catastrophic neurological events. (Source: National Blood Authority: Patient blood management guidelines)
source_refs: National Blood Authority: Patient blood management guidelines

options.text: Commence rituximab today as definitive treatment of the underlying disease
options.rationale: Rituximab is a component of standard treatment for this disease and will be needed, but given before viscosity is reduced it provokes a transient rise in immunoglobulin M in around half of patients, which can worsen hyperviscosity dangerously. It is withheld until plasma exchange has lowered the paraprotein. (Source: HSANZ: Waldenstrom macroglobulinaemia guidance)

options.text: Commence high dose dexamethasone alone and arrange a bone marrow biopsy tomorrow
options.rationale: Corticosteroid has activity against the clone and a marrow biopsy is required to confirm the diagnosis and guide treatment. Neither acts quickly enough to reverse the retinal and cerebral effects of hyperviscosity, which are reversible over hours with exchange and can become permanent if left. (Source: HSANZ: Waldenstrom macroglobulinaemia guidance)

options.text: Perform therapeutic venesection to lower the viscosity before any other treatment
options.rationale: Removing whole blood does lower viscosity in polycythaemia, where the excess red cell mass is the cause and the haematocrit is high. Here viscosity is driven by a plasma protein and the haemoglobin is already 72 g/L, so venesection would deepen the anaemia while leaving the paraprotein untouched. (Source: HSANZ: Waldenstrom macroglobulinaemia guidance)

explanation.summary: Hyperviscosity syndrome arises when a large paraprotein load raises plasma viscosity enough to impair microcirculatory flow, and it is far more common with immunoglobulin M than with other classes because the pentameric molecule is very large and remains largely within the intravascular compartment. The clinical triad is mucosal bleeding, visual disturbance and neurological symptoms ranging from headache and vertigo to seizures and coma, and the most specific physical sign is the fundoscopic appearance of dilated tortuous retinal veins with segmental constrictions, sometimes described as sausage shaped. Laboratory clues include marked rouleaux, a very high erythrocyte sedimentation rate, a large gap between total protein and albumin and a spuriously low sodium in some assays. Plasma exchange is the emergency treatment and relieves symptoms within hours, after which definitive treatment of the underlying disease is started. Two interventions can make things acutely worse: red cell transfusion, which raises whole blood viscosity and is deferred until viscosity has been lowered, and rituximab, which causes a transient immunoglobulin M flare in roughly half of patients.
key_points: Immunoglobulin M causes hyperviscosity at lower concentrations than other classes
Mucosal bleeding, visual disturbance and neurological symptoms form the triad
Dilated segmented retinal veins on fundoscopy are the most specific physical sign
Plasma exchange relieves symptoms within hours and is the emergency treatment
Both red cell transfusion and rituximab can acutely worsen hyperviscosity
explanation.pearls: Look at the gap between total protein and albumin before anything else when the erythrocyte sedimentation rate is above 100 mm/h: a globulin fraction approaching 80 g/L points to a paraprotein, and in that setting the two units of blood already prescribed for the anaemia are the most dangerous thing on the drug chart.

sources.label: National Blood Authority: Patient blood management guidelines
